title: Count vowels and consonants in a string (loop through each character, check if a/e/i/o/u).
shortTitle: Count vowels and consonants in a string

s1_definition.profdef: Counting vowels and consonants is a single linear pass where you examine each character, classify it as a vowel if it is one of a, e, i, o, u, as a consonant if it is any other letter, and ignore anything that is not a letter such as digits and spaces. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space because you keep just two counters.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants a quick readability metric on Rajesh's chosen account nickname. A clerk reads each letter of the nickname and makes a tally in the "vowel" column for a, e, i, o, u and in the "consonant" column for the rest, skipping any numbers or spaces.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk the string once, tally vowels and consonants, and skip anything that is not a letter.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Counting vowels and consonants is a single linear pass where you examine each character, classify it as a vowel if it is one of a, e, i, o, u, as a consonant if it is any other letter, and ignore anything that is not a letter such as digits and spaces. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space because you keep just two counters.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India wants a quick readability metric on Rajesh's chosen account nickname. A clerk reads each letter of the nickname and makes a tally in the "vowel" column for a, e, i, o, u and in the "consonant" column for the rest, skipping any numbers or spaces.

**One line to remember:** Walk the string once, tally vowels and consonants, and skip anything that is not a letter.

sections.s2_technical:
You keep two integer counters, both starting at zero. You loop over each character, usually after lowercasing so you only test five vowel letters instead of ten. For each character you first check it is a letter with `Character.isLetter(c)`; if it is not a letter, you skip it so digits and punctuation do not inflate either count. If it is a letter, you test whether it is a vowel, and if so increment the vowel counter, otherwise increment the consonant counter.

A clean way to test vowels is a helper such as `"aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0`, which returns a non-negative index when the character is found. Lowercasing first means you do not need to list both cases. Only counting characters that pass the isLetter check is the detail that separates correct code from naive code, because a nickname like "SAV 2001" contains a space and digits that are neither vowel nor consonant.

Time is O(n) for the single pass and space is O(1) for the two counters. This generalises easily: you could extend it to count digits or whitespace with more counters, but the core pattern of classify-and-tally stays the same.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India lets Rajesh set an account nickname and wants a small analytics panel showing how many vowels and consonants it contains. The system must count both. This is exactly how the vowel-consonant count works — classify each letter and tally.

Problem 2 — Nicknames can include digits and spaces, like "Rajesh 01", and those must not be counted as consonants. This is exactly why we check isLetter first and skip anything that is not a letter.

The code has a `TextAnalyzer` class with a `countVowelsAndConsonants` method returning a small result holder. The demo analyses a nickname.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: nickname `"Rajesh 01"`, lowercased to `"rajesh 01"`.

Step 1 — `'r'` is a letter, not a vowel: consonants becomes 1.

Step 2 — `'a'` is a vowel: vowels becomes 1.

Step 3 — `'j'` consonant: consonants 2.

Step 4 — `'e'` vowel: vowels 2.

Step 5 — `'s'` consonant: consonants 3.

Step 6 — `'h'` consonant: consonants 4.

Step 7 — `' '` is not a letter: skipped.

Step 8 — `'0'` and `'1'` are not letters: skipped.

Step 9 — Final counts vowels 2, consonants 4. Return and log.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Nickname 'Rajesh 01' → vowels=2, consonants=4
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: "Rajesh 01" → lowercase "rajesh 01"
    │
    ▼
  TextAnalyzer.countVowelsAndConsonants()
    │ r→cons(1)  a→vowel(1)  j→cons(2)  e→vowel(2)
    │ s→cons(3)  h→cons(4)   ' '→skip   0→skip  1→skip
    ▼
  LetterCount{ vowels=2, consonants=4 }
    │
    ▼
  Log: "vowels=2, consonants=4"
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting vowels and consonants is a single linear pass with two counters. I lowercase the string so I only have to test five vowel letters, then I loop through each character. For each character I first check whether it is a letter at all, and if it is not a letter I skip it, so digits, spaces, and punctuation do not pollute the counts. If it is a letter I test whether it is one of a, e, i, o, u, incrementing the vowel counter if so and the consonant counter otherwise. The whole thing is linear time and constant space.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this in a small analytics panel that shows how many vowels and consonants a customer's account nickname contains. Rajesh can set a nickname, and the panel breaks down its letters.

The detail I emphasise is the isLetter guard. Nicknames frequently contain digits and spaces, like Rajesh followed by a number, and a naive implementation that only checks for vowels and treats everything else as a consonant would wrongly count the digits and the space as consonants. By checking that the character is a letter first and skipping it otherwise, the counts stay accurate, which is the difference between a toy solution and one I would ship.
